AMAZON INDIGENOUS LAND DISPUTE

By: Latashia Naidoo | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
E-commerce giant, Amazon, is in a David vs Goliath battle with South Africa's so-called 'first people' over indigenous land they're now building their R4bn African headquarters on.

Unique Selling Point:
Indigenous leaders claim that the land on which Amazon's African HQ is being developed is "a sacred, environmentally-sensitive precinct" which belongs to their ancestors and their shared humanity. It is an epicentre of spirituality and resistance, where occupation and dispossession of the Two Rivers, it’s confluence and embankments occurred in 1657.
It is from this site where the First Frontier Wars were fought. And they now want it to be legally recognized and preserved as such.

Summary:
A groundswell of unhappiness has emerged for some of SA's first inhabitants — members of the Khoi and San - over a verdant patch of land in Cape Town that’s now been earmarked for US retail giant Amazon’s R4-billion African headquarters.
As development for the project gets underway, the former site of the River Club in Observatory is now a scene of conflict.

Cultural activists claim the development will place 150,000m² of concrete on a flood plain of high environmental sensitivity and huge heritage significance for first nation Khoi groups, and infill a sacred river.

According to Tauriq Jenkins of the Goringhaicona Khoena Council, a Khoi traditional group opposed to the project, they want the site – “where the land was first stolen by the Dutch (settlers) – to be declared a World Heritage Site.

The land, which has been earmarked for a multi-billion rand mixed-use development, comprising hotel, retail offices and residential units, has also faced a backlash from other community leaders, environmentalists and activists.

In recent months they have held marches at the site, and are demanding that the development be stopped immediately.

But Liesbeek Leisure Properties Trust (LLTP), the structure set up to develop the project, say the development went through an extensive public approval procedure, and that there have only been a “handful of vocal objectors”. He added that the company will also pay tribute to Khoi and San culture and history, by including an indigenous garden and a heritage centre where Khoi and San descendants will work as operators and educators.

However, the development is being fiercely opposed by more than 60 indigenous first nation entities, civic associations and environmental NGOs.

Further information:
In early-August 2021, rights groups filed an urgent interdict at the Western Cape High Court to halt the multi-billion development.
56,000 people have already signed a petition opposing the building plans on land, based on its archeological value.
